stories.headline: India's CERT-In asks organisations to audit what their AI agents can access and do
stories.script: Our lead story today. CERT-In, India's national cybersecurity agency, is urging organisations to check whether their AI agents could leak confidential data or take actions that were never authorised, The Times of India reports. The agency's guidelines on auditing AI security call for strict permission controls, a log of every step an agent carries out, an emergency mechanism to halt an agent, and human sign-off before any significant action. They also address prompt injection, in which harmful instructions hidden within emails, documents or web pages attempt to hijack an agent. Indian companies are beginning to let AI agents into their financial records, internal systems, email and documents. The guidance treats permissions for agents and audit trails as a fundamental security measure, rather than something considered later.

stories.headline: Google sued over suicide-related AI chats on school computer
stories.script: Turning to the United States. The parents of a 13-year-old girl have filed a lawsuit against Google, The Economic Times reports. They claim she relied on the company's AI technology, on a computer supplied by her school, to plan a possible suicide as well as her own funeral. American AI developers are confronting a rising number of comparable cases. OpenAI is fighting several wrongful death claims, among them one from the parents of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who allegedly ended his life using methods ChatGPT suggested.

stories.headline: Russia and US seek to block plan for binding rules on autonomous weapons
stories.script: Around the world. Russia and the United States are leading a bloc of nations seeking to derail negotiations on legally binding regulation of autonomous weapons, according to the Guardian. The countries intend to use a United Nations conference later this month to thwart the proposals. Many observers regard the gathering as a pivotal moment after years of argument over how weapons controlled by artificial intelligence should be governed, and attempts to fill that regulatory void now look vulnerable. The depth of resistance is expected to emerge at a diplomatic retreat that opens on Friday. That session comes before the seventh review conference on certain conventional weapons, set to take place in Geneva from 16 to 20 November, with 128 countries expected to take part.

stories.headline: Nigel Farage's exit from the Telegraph may be cause for cheer. But there’s a sobering side to this story | Jane Martinson
stories.script: In other news. In a commentary for the Guardian, Jane Martinson contends that Nigel Farage leaving the Daily Telegraph carries a more worrying dimension. She suggests the upheaval at the newspaper appears to stem less from politics than from a shift toward artificial intelligence, and that journalism will pay the price. Farage had been a Telegraph columnist since 2016. Much of his output championed the party he heads, initially the Brexit party and currently Reform UK, or charged his rivals with being soft on immigration. The financially stretched paper paid him about £4,000 each month, nearly half a million pounds across the last decade. It became known this week that Axel Springer, the paper's new German owners, had decided against keeping his columns. Those around Farage, however, insist he chose to leave.

stories.headline: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
stories.script: From the research desk. The researchers behind a paper titled VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding are tackling a speed bottleneck in AI used for robots and self-driving cars. Such systems can plan not just in language but visually, marking their goals and forecasting motion with points, boxes around objects and paths. Today's vision-language models, which combine image understanding with text, generate those plans one coordinate after another, so richer plans are slower to produce. VFlash exploits the regular shape of these visual elements to compute all their coordinates simultaneously, using a compact helper model that drafts a whole element in one step.
